consensus_summary: When figurative, islands/isles most commonly represent distant coastlands and their peoples, especially remote Gentile nations or the ends of the earth. Literal geography and islands displaced in cosmic judgment are major contextual alternatives.
book_summary: An island represents a distinct, set-apart people emerging from the sea of nations, receptive to God's law and preserved amid the collapse of surrounding kingdoms.
book_core_identification: A set-apart and preserved people distinguished from the surrounding nations.
boundary_disagreement: The book reclassifies passages about isles waiting for God's law from references to remote Gentile peoples into a symbol of a separated, protected people. It also incorporates judgment imagery into the definition, treating surrounding kingdoms as falling while the island-people is preserved.
material_contradiction: The central referent changes from the distant nations themselves to a distinct people separated out from the sea of nations. Moreover, Revelation 16:20 says every island flees in judgment, whereas the entry characterizes the island as preserved while other kingdoms fall.
rationale: This is not merely a narrower version of the consensus identification: it replaces the consensus's geographic-ethnic referent with an ecclesial or remnant-like community. The idea is not novel because the blind responses mention the rare allegorical interpretation of an island as the church, believer, or protected spiritual community amid the sea of nations. Nevertheless, that alternative is materially different from the dominant consensus core.
strongest_objection: Isaiah 42:4 and 51:5 naturally identify the isles with distant peoples awaiting God's rule, while Genesis 10:5 explicitly calls them Gentile territories. None of the printed texts clearly says that an island rises from a symbolic sea or remains preserved when other kingdoms fall; Revelation 16:20 instead depicts every island as fleeing.
